triage.reason: Classic pediatric presentation with barking cough and inspiratory stridor; diagnosis made clinically with important airway look-alikes.

demographics: Most common in children 6 months to 3 years of age
More frequent in fall and winter

risk_factors.text: Recent upper respiratory infection in the child or household contacts
Attending daycare or having older siblings in school

social_history: Exposure to other children with colds at daycare or home
exposures: Household or daycare contacts with recent cold symptoms

chief_complaints.text: My child has a barking cough that sounds like a seal
He makes a noisy, high-pitched sound when he breathes in
The cough is much worse at night

hpi.onset: Starts like a common cold with runny nose and mild cough, then over 1–2 days the cough becomes barking and breathing becomes noisy
hpi.duration: Symptoms usually last about 3–5 days, often worst on nights 2–3
hpi.progression: Cough and hoarseness worsen over the first day or two, then gradually improve; symptoms typically flare at night and settle during the day
hpi.location: Throat and upper chest; the noisy breathing comes from the neck/upper airway
hpi.quality: Barking, seal-like cough; harsh high-pitched inspiratory noise; hoarse or raspy cry and voice
hpi.severity: Usually mild to moderate; the child may be comfortable between coughing spells but distressed when the cough starts
hpi.timing: Worse at night and when the child is upset or crying; better when calm
relieving: Cool night air or sitting in a steamy bathroom (often reported by parents)

associated_symptoms.text: Noisy breathing that is worse when the child is active or upset
Retractions or belly breathing when working hard to breathe

pertinent_negatives: Stridor that is present at rest and does not change with position or crying
Sudden onset while eating or choking

positives.text: Noisy breathing worse with activity or crying

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants under 6 months may have milder classic barking cough but can develop severe upper airway obstruction quickly; they may present with poor feeding, irritability and apnea rather than a clear cough.
Older children and adolescents can get croup but it is less common; symptoms may be milder and more like a bad cold with hoarseness.
Immunocompromised children may have a more prolonged or severe course and are at higher risk for bacterial superinfection or atypical pathogens.

general.mild: Alert, playful, comfortable between coughing spells; no stridor at rest
general.moderate: Irritable and clingy; audible stridor at rest that eases when calm; mild retractions
general.severe: Distressed, anxious, sitting forward; marked retractions and nasal flaring; stridor at rest
general.critical: Lethargic or agitated with decreasing respiratory effort; pale or cyanotic; may have stridor that becomes quieter as obstruction worsens

findings.maneuver: Ask the child to cough, or observe a spontaneous cough
Auscultate over the neck and trachea while the child breathes quietly
Observe and listen while the child is calm and at rest
findings.finding: Stridor present at rest, indicating significant upper airway obstruction

findings.maneuver: Listen to the child's voice or cry
Observe the suprasternal notch during inspiration
Observe the chest wall during inspiration
findings.finding: Intercostal and subcostal retractions, nasal flaring, or belly breathing

findings.maneuver: Observe the mouth and oropharynx without using a tongue blade
Observe mouth opening and ability to swallow

findings.finding: Child is nontoxic and interactive when calm

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs during quiet breathing
Gently assess neck mobility when the child is calm

labs.caveat: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; the white count is often normal or only mildly elevated and does not distinguish viral croup from bacterial tracheitis.
Lymphocyte predominance is typical of a viral illness but is nonspecific.
Usually normal or mildly elevated; a markedly high value should raise concern for bacterial tracheitis or pneumonia.
Not routine; a normal value supports a viral cause when bacterial tracheitis is being considered.

imaging.preferred_when: Atypical features or concern for an alternative diagnosis such as epiglottitis or a foreign body

findings.text: Subglottic narrowing (steeple sign) on the anteroposterior view
Normal epiglottis and vallecula on the lateral view
Loss of the normal subglottic air column contour
Normal study despite clinically evident croup

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pneumonia or an inhaled foreign body

findings.text: Radio-opaque foreign body or asymmetric lung volumes

imaging.preferred_when: Recurrent, atypical, or severe croup where another cause of upper airway obstruction is suspected

findings.text: Subglottic narrowing with normal supraglottic structures

initial.why: Assesses oxygenation; hypoxemia is uncommon in uncomplicated croup and suggests another diagnosis
Looks for subglottic narrowing and helps exclude epiglottitis or a foreign body
initial.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain, the course is atypical, or an alternative cause of upper airway obstruction is suspected

supporting.why: Supports a viral cause and screens for a marked leukocytosis suggesting bacterial tracheitis
supporting.only_if: the child appears more ill than typical croup or has a high fever

supporting.why: A markedly elevated value raises concern for bacterial tracheitis or pneumonia
Evaluates for pneumonia or an inhaled foreign body
supporting.only_if: hypoxemia, focal lung findings, or an atypical course is present

not_indicated.why: No established role in typical croup
Not needed unless the child is dehydrated or severely ill
Bacteremia is not a feature of viral croup
Does not change management of typical croup

decision_points: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; avoid agitating the child with unnecessary tests or throat examination
Do not examine the throat with a tongue blade or attempt to visualize the epiglottis when epiglottitis is a concern
Stridor at rest, retractions, or hypoxemia indicate moderate to severe croup and warrant immediate treatment and monitoring
Consider epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, or anaphylaxis when drooling, toxic appearance, sudden onset, or lack of response to treatment is present

differential.name: Epiglottitis
differential.why_considered: Acute upper airway obstruction in a young child with stridor and respiratory distress
differential.trigger: Drooling, difficulty swallowing, muffled voice, high fever, or a toxic child sitting forward with the neck extended

history: Rapid onset over hours rather than days
High fever
Severe sore throat and refusal to swallow
No barking cough
exam: Drooling and inability to swallow secretions
Tripod or sniffing position, sitting forward
Stridor that is soft and does not improve with calming
labs: Blood cultures may grow Haemophilus influenzae type b or another bacterial pathogen
imaging: Lateral neck x-ray shows a thickened, rounded epiglottis (thumb sign) and normal subglottic airway
Direct visualization shows a swollen, cherry-red epiglottis

differential.name: Bacterial tracheitis
differential.why_considered: Child with croup-like barking cough and stridor who is more ill than typical viral croup
differential.trigger: High fever, toxic appearance, or worsening stridor despite racemic epinephrine and steroids

history: Often follows a viral upper respiratory infection
Rapidly worsening respiratory distress
Poor response to standard croup treatment
exam: Stridor at rest that persists after treatment
labs: Elevated inflammatory markers such as CRP
Tracheal secretions may grow Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus species
imaging: Neck x-ray may show subglottic narrowing but also irregular tracheal contour or membrane
Bronchoscopy shows purulent tracheal secretions and mucosal ulceration or pseudomembranes

differential.name: Foreign body aspiration
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset of cough, stridor, or noisy breathing in a young child
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset while eating or playing, or a witnessed choking episode

history: Sudden onset rather than a cold-like prodrome
Choking or gagging episode
No fever or preceding runny nose
exam: Asymmetric breath sounds or focal wheeze
Stridor or wheeze that does not respond to racemic epinephrine
labs: Normal white count and inflammatory markers
imaging: Chest x-ray may show a radio-opaque object, air trapping, or asymmetric lung volumes
Neck or chest x-ray may be normal; bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic

differential.name: Anaphylaxis
differential.why_considered: Acute stridor and respiratory distress in a child
differential.trigger: Exposure to a known allergen with rapid onset of stridor, hives, or hypotension

history: Exposure to food, medication, or insect sting minutes to hours before symptoms
Rapid progression over minutes
Associated itching, hives, or gastrointestinal symptoms
labs: No specific routine labs needed for diagnosis

differential.name: Bronchiolitis
differential.why_considered: Young child with cough, noisy breathing, and low-grade fever, especially in winter

history: Cough and congestion with prominent wheezing rather than barking cough
No hoarse voice
Often younger than 12 months
labs: Respiratory viral panel may identify RSV
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or shows hyperinflation; not routine

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Child with cough and noisy breathing that worsens at night

history: Recurrent episodes of wheeze and cough
Known triggers such as exercise, allergens, or cold air
No barking cough or hoarse voice
labs: Allergy testing or spirometry may support the diagnosis later
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal; not routine

differential.name: Retropharyngeal abscess
differential.why_considered: Child with fever, neck stiffness, and noisy breathing
differential.trigger: Fever with neck stiffness, refusal to move the neck, or drooling

history: High fever and severe neck pain
Refusal to move the neck or turn the head
No barking cough
imaging: Lateral neck x-ray shows widened retropharyngeal soft tissue space
CT with contrast shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection

differential.name: Laryngomalacia
differential.why_considered: Infant with noisy breathing and stridor

history: Stridor present since birth or the first weeks of life
Worse when lying on the back, feeding, or crying
No barking cough or fever
exam: High-pitched inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine
imaging: Flexible laryngoscopy shows omega-shaped epiglottis and prolapsing arytenoids

severity.mild: Barking cough and hoarse voice with no stridor at rest; child is comfortable, playful, and feeding well
severity.moderate: Inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when calm, mild retractions, and some irritability; child still interactive
severity.severe: Stridor at rest with marked retractions, nasal flaring, and agitation or distress; child may be tiring
severity.critical: Decreasing respiratory effort with lethargy or agitation, pallor or cyanosis, and quiet or absent stridor as obstruction worsens; impending respiratory failure

red_flags.meaning: Significant upper airway obstruction; needs immediate treatment and monitoring

red_flags.finding: Retractions, nasal flaring, or belly breathing
red_flags.meaning: Increased work of breathing; moderate to severe croup
Suggests epiglottitis or another supraglottic process; do not examine the throat
Suggests bacterial tracheitis or another bacterial infection

red_flags.finding: Stridor that becomes quieter or absent while the child worsens
red_flags.meaning: Worsening obstruction with decreasing air movement; a late and dangerous sign

red_flags.finding: Sudden onset while eating or choking

complications.name: Upper airway obstruction with respiratory failure
Bacterial superinfection such as bacterial tracheitis or pneumonia

special_populations.differences: Infants under 6 months may have a milder barking cough but can develop severe upper airway obstruction quickly; they may present with poor feeding, irritability, and apnea rather than classic stridor.
Older children and adolescents can get croup but it is less common; symptoms may be milder and more like a bad cold with hoarseness.
Immunocompromised children may have a more prolonged or severe course and are at higher risk for bacterial superinfection or atypical pathogens.

key_questions.question: What does the cough sound like?
key_questions.looking_for: A barking, seal-like cough rather than a wet or wheezing cough

key_questions.question: Do you hear a high-pitched noise when your child breathes in?
key_questions.looking_for: Inspiratory stridor, and whether it is present only with crying or also at rest

key_questions.question: How did this start and how has it changed over the last day or two?
key_questions.looking_for: Cold-like prodrome followed by barking cough and hoarseness over 1–2 days; rapid worsening over hours suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Is the noisy breathing worse at night or when your child is upset?
key_questions.looking_for: Nighttime and crying-related worsening, typical of croup

key_questions.question: Is your child drooling or having trouble swallowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Drooling or refusal to swallow suggests epiglottitis; do not examine the throat

key_questions.question: Did this start suddenly while your child was eating or playing, or was there a choking episode?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset or choking suggests foreign body aspiration

key_questions.question: How is your child acting between coughing spells — playful and interactive, or lethargic and struggling to breathe?
key_questions.looking_for: Comfortable and interactive suggests mild croup; lethargy, agitation, or continuous distress suggests severe obstruction

key_questions.question: Has your child been drinking and making normal amounts of urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Decreased intake or fewer wet diapers suggests dehydration

key_questions.question: Any fever, runny nose, or hoarse voice or cry?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever, congestion, and hoarseness supporting a viral cause

key_questions.question: Has your child had episodes like this before, and have they ever needed treatment in the emergency department?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent croup raises concern for an underlying airway problem such as laryngomalacia or subglottic stenosis

key_questions.question: Is anyone else at home or daycare sick with a cold?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent upper respiratory infection in household or daycare contacts

key_questions.question: Has your child been exposed to cigarette smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondhand smoke exposure, a risk factor for croup

key_questions.question: Does your child have any allergies, or could this be a reaction to a food, medicine, or insect sting?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapid onset after allergen exposure with hives or wheezing suggests anaphylaxis

key_questions.question: Any rash, vomiting, diarrhea, or neck stiffness?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in typical croup; present findings point to an alternative diagnosis

reasoning_points: Young child, typically 6 months to 3 years, with a recent cold-like illness
Barking, seal-like cough with hoarse voice or cry
High-pitched inspiratory stridor that worsens with crying, agitation, or nighttime
Symptoms worse at night and over 3–5 days, often worst on nights 2–3
Child is nontoxic and comfortable between coughing spells, with no drooling or difficulty swallowing
No expiratory wheezing or crackles, arguing against bronchiolitis or asthma
Diagnosis is clinical; imaging and labs are reserved for atypical or severe presentations
Epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, foreign body aspiration, and anaphylaxis considered and excluded

easy: Toddler with a classic barking cough and hoarse voice after a few days of runny nose
Stridor only when crying or upset, resolving when calm
Low-grade fever and otherwise well-appearing child
medium: Stridor present at rest with mild retractions, requiring treatment and monitoring
Infant under 6 months with poor feeding and irritability rather than a clear barking cough
Older child with milder symptoms that resemble a bad cold with hoarseness
Recurrent nighttime episodes with normal examination during the day
hard: Child with high fever and toxic appearance whose stridor does not improve after racemic epinephrine and steroids, suggesting bacterial tracheitis
Sudden onset of stridor while eating or playing, suggesting foreign body aspiration
Drooling, muffled voice, and refusal to swallow, suggesting epiglottitis
Rapid onset of stridor with hives or wheezing after allergen exposure, suggesting anaphylaxis
Child with recurrent croup raising concern for an underlying airway abnormality such as subglottic stenosis
